A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same response-time preference-learning framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite additions and pagination changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic linear and neural-network experiments, semi-synthetic Pick-a-Pic experiments, and an unknown-barrier sensitivity study in Figures 1–3 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds participant-based food-preference bandit results in Appendix D.1 and Table 3.

M1.justification: The losses, nuisance-estimation procedures, architectures, and Meta-Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Appendix D.1 adds a procedural adaptation: inserting the orthogonal-loss estimator into Li et al.'s sequential-elimination algorithm in place of its response-time estimator.

E1.justification: Appendix D.1 adds food-preference data containing choices and response times from 42 participants and constructs adaptive best-arm-identification tasks. This substantially extends the previous synthetic reward-estimation and semi-synthetic image-preference coverage to another domain, population, and task.

E2.justification: The existing log-loss, non-orthogonal-loss, and orthogonal variants remain. New Table 3 directly compares against the LZR+24 response-time method and a Preference Only bandit baseline. Newly discussed Gaussian-process methods are cited but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The added bandit experiment introduces participant-specific sequential elimination, total sample budgets of 500, 1000, and 1500, and a selection-probability outcome. This is a substantial additional evaluation design beyond passive reward estimation. The previously documented supervised training and test settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 1 revises the sensitivity analysis of estimation error versus reward magnitude, changing its curves and omitting the previously plotted magnitudes 4 and 6. The unknown-barrier study in Appendix A.4 and the neural-network data-splitting versus data-reuse comparison remain.

E5.justification: Figure 1 changes its uncertainty label from standard deviation to standard error. Figures 2 and 3 newly specify standard error and standard deviation, respectively. Appendix D.1 adds 70 independent trials per participant and participant-level quartile summaries; the repetition counts for retained experiments are unchanged.

E6.justification: Figure 1 substantially revises reported errors: at the same stated d=10, n=8000, and reward magnitude 15, orthogonal error changes from approximately 0.4 to 1.9 and non-orthogonal error from 0.9 to 3.2. Table 3 adds bandit results, but its 'correctly incorrectly' caption conflicts with the prose's correct-selection interpretation. Figure 3 and Tables 1–2 retain their results.

T1.justification: Theorem C.5 and Corollaries 5.3–5.4 change the truncation-bias contribution from linear to squared. Corollary 5.3 gains a truncation-threshold factor, and Appendix C corrects the Markov-bound exponent and the empirical-minimizer inequality in the data-splitting proof. These refine existing finite-sample arguments; the principal orthogonality and asymptotic results remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and four principal contribution statements retain their meaning. The introduction adds a claim that substituting the proposed estimator into Li et al.'s sequential-elimination algorithm improves best-arm identification, extending the claimed empirical applicability beyond supervised reward estimation.

C2.justification: New Section 7 explicitly identifies robustness concerns involving noisy response times and population-dependent rewards and barriers, and treats adaptive regret minimization as future work. Appendix D.1 also interprets the new comparison as showing larger benefits at smaller budgets, although its metric-label conflict limits that interpretation.

D1.justification: v1's anonymized Google Drive code pointer is replaced by a named GitHub repository link in Section 6. The Appendix D code footnote is left incomplete. Existing architecture, nuisance-training, and data-generation details are otherwise retained; the PDFs alone do not establish whether either external resource is accessible.

R1.justification: A new Other Related Work discussion substantially expands positioning against dueling and logistic bandits and Gaussian-process response-time models. It adds corresponding citations and explicit distinctions concerning adaptive sampling, reward estimation, high-dimensional applicability, and likelihood-free versus variational inference. Li et al. was already discussed in v1.

P1.justification: v2 expands the title, adds related-work discussion, a conclusion, acknowledgments, and Appendix D.1, and locally rewrites Appendix C explanations. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact, so this is a limited structural and editorial revision.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn with revised uncertainty displays and labels, and Figures 2–3 receive expanded captions. Figure placement changes, and Table 3 adds three budget-specific panels. The overall document template and existing table structures remain.

improvement.justification: v2 makes useful finite-sample corrections, clarifies uncertainty reporting, and broadens research positioning. However, its principal new empirical extension is internally inconsistent: Appendix D.1 describes correct-selection probabilities, Table 3 says 'correctly incorrectly,' and the reported Ours values are lower. This prevents reliable interpretation of the claimed bandit advantage. The benefits and this material weakness in the added evidence leave the net quality change uncertain.
